blocks.content: The Tenth Schedule was inserted in the Constitution by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1985.

rows: Not allowed to join any political party
Joins any political party after election
Allowed within 6 months of taking seat
Joins a political party after 6 months

items: The decision on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is made by the Speaker/Chairman, NOT the President or Governor.
In the Kihoto Hollohan case (1992), the Supreme Court ruled that the decision of the Speaker/Chairman is subject to Judicial Review.
The 91st Amendment Act of 2003 abolished the 'split' provision (1/3rd members) as a defense against disqualification.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1985 to prevent political defections.
The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act of 2003 removed the exception for splits and strengthened the anti-defection provisions.
Members face disqualification for voluntarily giving up party membership or voting against party whip without condonation within 15 days.
Independent members are disqualified if they join any political party after election.
Nominated members can join a political party within six months, but face disqualification if they join after six months.
Disqualification decisions are made by the Speaker or Chairman of the House and are subject to judicial review.
